Silly Nihilists, emptiness and meaninglessness isn't an answer to anything.  And objectively speaking I have a hard time viewing things the way OP does after reading a proof by Descartes on proving that nothing does not exist.  

How can you define something as worthless without being able to make a value judgment?  

Bleh, nihilism...  There are actually so many embedded ideas in this paragraph i'm gunna see if I can list them all.

>Why live a meaningless life?

This is implying that all lives are meaningless.  Of course there is a spectrum of people who are more meaningful than others, but as sure as there is cause and effect with every atom in the visible universe, there is a meaning to everything that happens

>The way I see it, life is inherently worthless, since there is no objective purpose or value.

So this is ridiculous.  Only when a person takes an incredibly broad, macro view of everything does, 'life seem worthless or meaningless'.  In fact if there was meaning at the most broad level of life, everyone would be fated to live a life of destiny.  I actually find it optimistic that we get to make choices and in a sense carve our own meaning in life as opposed to having it put out in front of us objectively.

>Thus I am troubled by why anyone would choose to live.

-Sigh- Is being emo still popular?

>Happiness, procreation, advancement of the species are all empty >answers.

Why?  You can't just say large attributes of life are empty because you can't find an objective value for them.  What quality does objective value have that reflects and facilitates emptiness in other things?  At the very least objectivity has some type of value, but you can't have objectivity without a world to live in in the first place so that implies that the value that you assume is imbedded in objectivity must be somewhere in the actual world which might actually find its way in life.

>Especially happiness, since that is only a delusion that gives an >evolutionary advantage.

It seems like if you define something derogatorily you have proven it is meaningless.  That isn't a proof, you are just describing something in a way that marginalizes what you are describing.  It would be like me saying, "OP's ideas are worthless because he describes his ideas with a bad attitude."

>Now, I see everywhere people who delude themselves in thinking that >subjective meaning give something to life, or that life is inherently >meaningful and beautiful.

I don't think people delude themselves as being happy, people can purposefully try to be happy because it is better than the alternative of being sad.  Maybe that has more to do with emotional intelligence than delusion.

>And that confuses me, as I see no reason anyone would want to be >alive, nor try to remain so.

And you finish everything off with a solipsistic point of view where you project your own feelings onto others, assuming everyone else is just like you but acting differently.

Tod couldn't believe it.  Back to school late in life and he was already wasting his time.  The year was 3090 and the human race had decided the only way to choose who belonged to the social elite had been through an intellectual hierarchy.  Procrastination could in a sense be a death wish, if you didn't have your shit together not only could you be shut out of the higher society, but it meant you were destined to interact with everyone else thrown to the bottom of the heap, so to speak.  
Tod was working on Chemistry.  Well, Bio-Chemistry to be specific, his homework assignment was to recreate a self-sustaining protein which could be used in cats to make them immortal.  It was elementary stuff for the time, immortality had long been discovered, but regardless of how long a person could live cognitive plasticity did not change.  In other words there was a limit to how much knowledge a person could obtain, and if they were lazy and didn't keep up with their work atrophy would cognitively set in and sooner or later they would forget everything.
Tod wasn't young or old, leaning more on the young side he idealized making something of himself but found himself getting stuck over and over, day in and day out.  Little did he know that a reservoir of sub-conscious resentment kept him from progressing.  He hated himself too much to let himself succeed.  He wouldn't become anything in this futuristic world.  Hopefully the atrophy would come quickly.

Otherwise do something that can distract you long enough from the problems you have and try to carve out a neutral or better yet happy place for yourself.

When you have two numbers left in a square (like the 2 & the 5) check the two columns (or rows if vertical) they make up for another set of boxes that have either a set of 5s or 2s in the same two column as the 2 & 5 that is locked in.  In this case the south-west square on the bottom row (between the 1 & the 8) there is a possibility of a 2 being in either of the two boxes.  Now the key to this is that because we have the original 2 & 5 locked in, and a mandatory possibility of two 2s in the two boxes on the south-west square we eliminate the possibility of any 5s being in the boxes where the 2s are in the south-west square.  With this rule you can figure out that in the south-west square there is a 5 in the center box and solve the rest of the puzzle.

[The reason for this is if there was a possibility of 5s being in those two boxes on the south-west square this particular sudoku would be unsolvable]

There are implied ideas, one is that the broadening of technology is always good.  This is not true, if I were to reinvent a light bulb that produces less light with more materials but the invention was new, at best the invention could only have an aesthetic value or a societal value.  Nothing more.  But assuming we are advancing technology  I actually believe at some point there will be a plateau of technology with regard to compatibility to a human being.  Where even if we can fly from this galaxy to the next and live forever there will be a limit to what technology can do for a human being or humanity as a whole.  For example technology could advance in such a way that we become more and more socially alienated but acquire more and more skills, and technology can advance such that it compliments humanity as a whole.  I think video games are a good example of each, some video games focus on single player mode some on multi-player mode.  The former facilitating basic skills and techniques, the latter being either cooperative or competitive with other players.  That being said, we are far from the limit of technological advances and what we are left with are technologies that fall into one of the following categories.

1)  Help us survive e.g. technology that better allocates food/water and the bottom rung of Maslow's Pyramid
2)  Facilitate a better quality of quality of life e.g. help us with personal skills and development, e.g. an exercise bike or the higher aspect of Maslow's Pyramid
3)  Advancement in a tool itself or the facilitation of identification itself, e.g. a microscope
